title: Digital leadership from the perspective of dynamic capabilities: the effect on sustainable performance and resilience through agility.
paragraphs: Digital disruption has transformed organizations [ 79 ]. In today's rapidly evolving technological landscape, organizations need leaders who can keep up with digital developments to survive. Leaders' ability to navigate the digital world is associated with organizational success [ 19 ].

Digital leadership, derived from Hambrick and Mason's [ 27 ] Upper Echelons Theory, refers to the integration of leadership skills and digital competencies to leverage digital technologies for organizational change and innovation [ 22 , 84 ]. Such leaders are also associated with encouraging innovative approaches among employees, which in turn is associated with increased motivation and performance [ 19 ].

From an organizational psychology perspective, leadership behaviors go beyond being merely a set of actions; they are actively interpreted and understood psychologically by employees. This interpretation process occurs through collective psychological filters such as perceptions of psychological safety and organizational climate [ 17 , 69 ]. Ultimately, this process is associated with how employees interpret uncertainty, respond to change, and regulate their work-related behaviors. Recent studies have examined psychological mechanisms linking digital leadership to outcomes (e.g., [ 42 , 43 , 88 , 89 ]. The present study, however, focuses on organizational agility as a mediating mechanism within Dynamic Capabilities Theory, without directly measuring these psychological processes.

In organizations undergoing digital transformation, employees continuously evaluate leaders’ digital competencies in terms of perceived support, transparency, and responsiveness. These evaluations are associated with collective meaning-making processes, which in turn are associated with employees’ psychological readiness to adapt and learn [ 60 ]. Accordingly, perceived organizational agility and resilience may reflect shared psychological perceptions that are associated with reduced uncertainty and with sustainable performance [ 30 ].

Digital leadership is defined as a strategic approach that is associated with promoting innovation and collaboration through the effective use of technology, which in turn is associated with increased organizational efficiency and productivity [ 80 ]. This approach is not only associated with strengthening decision-making processes and contributing to organizational goals, but also is associated with employees' psychological experiences arising from their interaction with technology (in the context of basic needs such as autonomy, competence, and connectedness).

Organizational agility is a dynamic capability defined as the ability to quickly adapt to changing environmental conditions and deliver innovative, customer-centric solutions [ 32 ]. From a psychological perspective, this capability is associated with a mindset based on the collective tolerance of organizational members towards uncertainty and their interpretation of change as a learning opportunity rather than a threat. Organizational resilience, on the other hand, is the ability to quickly overcome crises, reallocate resources, optimize processes, and harmonize relationships, transforming challenges into growth opportunities [ 12 ]. These capabilities are also associated with employees’ ability to cope with stress and adapt to changing conditions.

Through digital transformation, organizations can not only respond quickly to crises but also are associated with improved employee sustainable performance while fulfilling their environmental responsibilities [ 71 ]. Recent studies, such as Lathabhavan and Kuppusamy [ 48 ], have demonstrated that digital leadership is associated with organizational resilience. However, these studies primarily focus on direct or single-mediator effects. In contrast, the present study extends this line of inquiry by proposing a dual mediation model in which organizational agility serves as the key mechanism through which digital leadership is simultaneously associated with both organizational resilience and employee sustainable performance. Unlike Lathabhavan and Kuppusamy [ 48 ], who examined employee empowerment as a mediator and organizational performance as the sole outcome in Indian SMEs during the acute COVID-19 crisis, our study introduces organizational agility as the mediating mechanism and models dual outcomes (resilience and sustainable performance) in a regular operating environment. Furthermore, while they drew on Conservation of Resources theory, we ground our model in Dynamic Capabilities Theory while considering psychological interpretations as a complementary perspective.

Nevertheless, the mechanisms through which digital leadership may be associated with employee sustainable performance and resilience have not been sufficiently investigated in a single integrated model. Furthermore, while the individual links between these constructs have been explored, there is a need for comprehensive models that integrate digital leadership, agility, resilience, and sustainable performance to clarify the underlying pathways, particularly the dual mediating role of agility.

This gap necessitates a deeper understanding of the human and psychological dimensions of digital transformation within an integrated framework. Moreover, the transformative impact of digitalization extends beyond internal capabilities, actively reshaping how organizations create value and engage with their broader ecosystem [ 26 ]. Consequently, we propose and test an integrated model (Fig. 1 ) grounded in Dynamic Capabilities Theory and organizational psychology. The model posits that digital leadership is positively associated with resilience and sustainable performance. It is associated with shared perceptions of agility and resilience, with agility serving as the observable manifestation of dynamic capabilities [ 75 ]. Thus, agility functions as the key mechanism through which digitally driven leadership is associated with tangible outcomes.

In order to adapt to constantly changing environmental conditions, organizations need to effectively manage the processes of integrating, directing, and restructuring their resources and competencies. Dynamic Capabilities Theory states that in uncertain and rapidly changing environments, organizations cannot rely solely on existing resources. In this context, organizations need to develop strategic flexibility to gain a sustainable competitive advantage [ 77 ].

Dynamic capabilities focus on the processes by which organizations perceive, evaluate, and transform their structures for sustainable competitive advantage through environmental opportunities [ 42 , 43 ]. Perceived digital leadership, through its strategic vision and technology-driven decision-making processes, is associated with building upon these foundations, and may be associated with fostering perceptual alertness and a learning mindset [ 83 ]. Dynamic capabilities are associated with organizational agility by accelerating strategic decision-making in uncertain market conditions [ 76 ],they are also associated with organizational resilience by providing flexible response capacity in crises [ 49 ].

From a psychological standpoint, these dynamic capabilities can be interpreted as being reflected in employees' shared cognitive schemas, collective interpretations of change, and motivation to engage in adaptive behaviors. The present study does not directly measure these cognitive and affective mechanisms; rather, it focuses on their hypothesized perceptual outcomes—namely, perceived organizational agility and resilience. Accordingly, these mechanisms are considered as a theoretical perspective and as potential avenues for future research. Recent empirical studies have explicitly modelled agility as a mediating dynamic capability pathway to resilience, whether in the context of resource scarcity [ 57 ], adaptive marketing capabilities during crises [ 4 ], or employee-level digital work engagement [ 8 ]. The micro-foundations of dynamic capabilities increasingly emphasize employee cognition and affect. Zhang et al. [ 89 ] show that digital leadership induces flow at work, enhancing cognitive flexibility (improvisational ability) and affective attachment (emotional commitment)—states critical for DCT's sensing and seizing processes. Zhang, Akhtar, et al. [ 88 ] demonstrate that responsible leadership drives exploitation and exploration knowledge search behaviors, directly supporting transforming capacity. Khan et al. [ 42 , 43 ]further link digital leadership to circular economy practices as tangible outcomes of dynamic capability deployment. Collectively, these studies suggest that digital leadership activates dynamic capabilities through interpretive pathways—shared perceptions of psychological safety, collective efficacy, and meaning-making— which suggest potential interpretive pathways that may underlie the relationships examined in our mediation model. Future research is needed to test these proposed mechanisms directly. Therefore, while Dynamic Capabilities Theory provides the overarching framework for why organizations need to adapt, this study adopts the view that the how of adaptation may involve employees' collective interpretations of leaders' actions and environmental shifts.

These capabilities link employee sustainable performance to organizational learning and long-term value creation [ 29 ]. Digital leadership strengthens these outcomes by integrating resources and increasing agility [ 7 , 32 , 59 ]. It is important to clarify how organizational agility is conceptualized in the present study. Drawing on Teece et al. [ 76 ], who view agility as an outcome of dynamic capabilities, we do not treat agility as a higher-order dynamic capability itself. Rather, we conceptualize organizational agility as the perceptual manifestation of an organization's underlying sensing, seizing, and transforming processes—specifically, the degree to which employees collectively perceive their organization as flexible, responsive, and fast in adapting to change. In our model, agility serves as a mediating mechanism through which digital leadership (an upper-echelon antecedent) is associated with organizational resilience and sustainable performance.

This study integrates the lens of the Upper Echelons Theory (UET) [ 27 ] with the Dynamic Capabilities Theory (DCT) to provide a multi-level theoretical explanation. UET posits that organizational outcomes reflect the cognitive bases and values of top leaders. In the context of digital transformation, leaders' digital competencies, strategic vision, and interpretations of technological change serve as an initiating mechanism that shapes the organization's development of dynamic capabilities.

Digital leadership can also be interpreted through the lens of Dynamic Capabilities Theory, particularly in terms of sensing, seizing, and transforming organizational capacities. In digitally intensive environments, leaders play a critical role not only in initiating technological change but also in enabling organizations to recognize emerging opportunities, respond rapidly to environmental uncertainty, and reconfigure internal processes accordingly. From this perspective, digital leadership functions as a strategic managerial capability that facilitates organizational adaptation and renewal. Organizational agility represents the perceptual and behavioral manifestation of these dynamic processes, reflecting the organization’s ability to respond flexibly and effectively to changing demands. In turn, resilience emerges as a longer-term strategic outcome of these adaptive capabilities, enabling organizations to maintain continuity and recover from disruptions under conditions of uncertainty.

Thus, digital leadership is conceptualized as an antecedent influencing employees’ perceptions of their organizational environment, which subsequently manifest as perceived organizational agility. While prior research has examined pairwise relationships in isolation, the present study brings these relationships together within a single model.

In the digital era, a business's ability to maintain a competitive edge and adapt to environmental changes is associated with organizational agility and digital leadership [ 18 ]. Leadership is considered fundamental to promoting agility, and the leadership style adopted in an organization is significantly associated with the development of organizational agility [ 64 ]. According to the Dynamic Capabilities Theory, businesses must effectively structure their resources to adapt to changing environmental conditions and maintain their competitive advantage [ 77 ]. Perceived digital leaders are associated with making strategic decisions by sensing environmental changes and facilitating organizational learning through innovative technologies. Thus, opportunities may be evaluated and strategies may be restructured [ 55 ].

Organizational agility refers to the ability of businesses to adapt quickly and effectively to the changes they face in the digital age. In today's competitive environment, this ability is considered a decisive factor for organizations. In this process, perceived digital leaders are considered crucial for guiding change, supporting innovative approaches, and making organizational structures more flexible [ 47 ]. Some studies in the literature address the relationship between digital leadership and organizational agility [ 38 , 59 ].

Therefore, agility may be cultivated through strategic restructuring and the adaptive climate that perceived digital leadership is associated with. Perceived digital leadership is positively associated with the organization's sensing and seizing capabilities, which in turn is associated with coordinated adaptation [ 17 ], (Parker & Grote, [ 60 ]). These processes can be viewed as a complementary perspective for understanding how perceived digital leadership is associated with agility at the perceptual level. Consistent with our conceptualization in the Dynamic Capabilities section, we treat agility as the perceptual manifestation of dynamic capabilities–-the emergent outcome of sensing, seizing, and transforming processes. In the age of digital transformation, digital leadership may also be associated with long-term employee sustainability through its association with adaptive and supportive work environments. Leaders who are perceived as influencing the achievement of societal and business goals are associated with continuity and growth through adapting to changing conditions ( [ 6 ]: 101). In this context, the concept of digital leadership stands out for its perceived ability to guide digital transformation and effectively utilize technological innovations. Organizational resilience is the capacity of businesses to survive and thrive during crises, economic fluctuations, and technological changes. According to the Dynamic Capabilities Theory, businesses' sustainable competitive advantage is associated with their capacity to perceive environmental changes and evaluate opportunities [ 77 ]. Digital leaders may be associated with organizations' adaptability by making decision-making processes more flexible and supporting resilience during crises. Digital competencies and technological innovations are associated with businesses' adaptation capacity and resilience [ 66 ].

Organizational resilience, therefore, extends beyond structural robustness to encompass a collective capacity to anticipate, absorb, and adapt to adversity. Digital leadership may be associated with this capacity through its association with coordination and effective use of technological resources. When employees perceive their leaders as digitally adept, this may be reflected in a shared belief in the organization's ability to navigate crises. Such perceptions may reduce uncertainty and support adaptive responses, thereby being associated with the organization's overall resilience [ 17 , 30 ]. [From a micro-foundational perspective, the relationship between digital leadership and resilience is further supported by evidence that responsible leadership is associated with sustainable performance through knowledge search mechanisms [ 88 ], and that psychological safety amplifies the positive effects of flow on adaptive outcomes [ 89 ]. Organizations need to have dynamic capabilities in order to effectively perceive and evaluate external opportunities. These capabilities are enacted through employees' cognitive evaluations, sensemaking processes, and shared interpretations of environmental change. Dynamic capabilities are considered an important source of competitive advantage [ 77 ]. Because these capabilities must be continuously renewed to respond to environmental changes, employees are required to sustain motivation, focus, and adaptive effort over time. Employee sustainable performance refers to both the long-term success of an organization and the ability of employees to maintain their performance through sustained commitment and adaptability. Therefore, organizations must sustain this performance not only at the structural level but also by enhancing employees' capacity to cope with change. Ultimately, this synergy between organizational structure and individual adaptability is the foundation of sustainable high performance [ 51 ].

The ability of organizations to sustain their competitive advantage is associated with their level of digital transformation adoption, which is associated with how employees experience work processes and cognitively evaluate organizational change. Digital leadership encompasses leadership approaches related to digital technologies and transformation processes, and is associated with organizational performance through innovative work behavior by being associated with employees' engagement and willingness to adapt [ 19 , 78 ]. The Dynamic Capabilities Theory considers the abilities to perceive, evaluate opportunities, and restructure as necessary for adaptation [ 75 ].

Digital leadership, by being associated with employees' creative skills, innovation capabilities, and dynamic competencies, is positively associated with their readiness, adaptability, and capacity for sustained effort–-thereby being associated with both long-term individual performance and organizational employee sustainable performance [ 44 , 68 ]. Accordingly, employee sustainable performance refers to both the long-term success of the organization and the ability of employees to maintain their performance through continuous commitment and adaptability. While several studies in the literature support the positive relationship between digital leadership and employee sustainable performance [ 2 , 20 , 44 ], it is important to note that the strength of this relationship may be context-dependent. For instance, Yahya et al., [ 86 ] found a non-significant direct association between digital leadership and sustainable performance in a public sector setting, suggesting that organizational or environmental factors may influence this link. To delineate the conceptual boundaries, we position dynamic capabilities as the overarching, higher-order theory explaining how organizations systematically adapt. Organizational agility is conceptualized as a specific, manifest dynamic capability–-the ability to sense and respond with speed and flexibility. It is the mediating mechanism through which the broader Dynamic Capabilities Theory processes are realized in our model. Organizational resilience, while also embodying adaptive capacity, is positioned primarily as a strategic outcome reflecting the organization's robustness and ability to recover from disruption. Resilience is not merely a capability but an enduring state resulting from the effective deployment of dynamic capabilities like agility. This study thus examines a sequential logic: Digital leadership is associated with organizational agility, which in turn is associated with resilience and sustainable performance.

Although organizational agility and resilience are closely related dynamic capabilities that both concern adaptation, they are theoretically distinct in their core focus and temporal orientation. Organizational agility primarily denotes the proactive capacity to sense and respond swiftly to environmental changes and opportunities, emphasizing speed, flexibility, and proactive innovation. Organizational resilience, conversely, centers on the reactive and absorptive capacity to withstand, recover from, and adapt following adversities or crises, emphasizing robustness, bounce-back ability, and sustained functioning. While agility is about navigating change for competitive advantage, resilience is about enduring disruption for survival and continuity. This theoretical distinction justifies their treatment as separate constructs in our model, a position supported by our empirical assessment of discriminant validity.

Organizational agility is associated with organizational resilience through its association with proactive responses to emerging risks and disruptions [ 53 ]. The relationship between organizational agility and resilience is grounded in Dynamic Capabilities Theory [ 77 ] and can also be interpreted through perceptual and behavioral processes. Agility is associated with collective experiences of successful adaptation, which may be associated with shared interpretations of change as manageable rather than threatening. Such interpretations may be associated with adaptive responses and may be associated with resilience over time [ 30 , 49 ]. Agile organizations are more likely to be associated with strengthening resilience by identifying opportunities and responding effectively [ 32 ].

These capabilities become more effective as employees' cognitive flexibility and readiness for change increase. Some studies in the literature address the relationship between organizational agility and organizational resilience [ 3 , 14 , 56 ]. This agility–resilience link is further supported by literature on workforce agility, which emphasizes the human and behavioral foundations of adaptive capacity. A socio-technical perspective suggests that for an organization to be agile and resilient, its workforce must possess the flexibility and adaptability required to navigate change [ 72 ]. Digital leadership and HR practices that are associated with such workforce agility are thus associated with building organizational-level resilience. Extending our conceptualization of agility as the observable manifestation of dynamic capabilities, we propose that this capacity also is associated with long-term individual and organizational outcomes. Organizational agility is a dynamic competency that can be learned and continuously accessed when necessary and is associated with business performance in a volatile market environment [ 82 ]. Agile organizations can respond quickly to the market through collaboration and external stakeholder support, thereby being associated with performance and being associated with process efficiency.

In this process, employees' openness to collaboration, attitudes toward uncertainty, and identification with organizational goals play a decisive role. Access to current technologies also is associated with employees' technological skills and overall performance [ 63 ]. Access to technology may be associated with employees' perceptions of competence and their confidence in their ability to perform work tasks effectively. According to the Dynamic Capabilities Theory, agile organizations adapt to environmental changes and are associated with developing their capabilities by continuously restructuring their resources [ 77 ]. This restructuring process is related to how employees interpret change and adapt to new conditions.

Perceived organizational agility is associated with businesses' competitive advantage and employee sustainable performance through being associated with their ability to respond quickly to environmental opportunities using their dynamic capabilities. From a perceptual perspective, agility may be linked to employees' ability to sustain performance over time through being associated with adaptive behaviors and effective task engagement. Some studies in the literature address the relationship between organizational agility and employee sustainable performance [ 36 , 40 , 41 ]. The rationale for positioning organizational agility as a mediator lies in its role as a core mechanism within the Dynamic Capabilities Theory framework. Digital leadership, through its strategic vision and digital competence, is associated with initiating the processes of sensing and seizing opportunities. However, for these leadership-driven initiatives to be reflected in resilience and sustained performance, they must be associated with organization-wide adaptive actions. Agility is seen as representing this operationalization–-the dynamic capability through which strategic intent is associated with speed, flexibility, and responsive action. Consistent with our earlier conceptualization, agility is treated here as the perceptual manifestation of these processes. Therefore, positioning agility as a mediator reflects the core proposition of our model: the influence of digital leadership on key outcomes is largely associated with its ability to be associated with activating this adaptive capability.

The relationship between digital leadership, perceived organizational resilience, and employee sustainable performance can be better understood when organizational agility is included as a mediating variable. Perceived organizational agility is defined as the ability to adapt quickly to changing conditions and plays a key role within the Resource-Based View and Dynamic Capabilities Theory. This ability reflects how employees interpret change, regulate uncertainty, and translate leadership cues into adaptive behavior. The Resource-Based View seeks to explain how organizations achieve sustainable competitive advantage [ 39 ], while the Dynamic Capabilities Theory emphasizes the adaptation of resources to changing conditions [ 75 , 77 ]. Thus, competitive advantage is associated not only with resource possession but also with employees' capacity to engage with and adapt these resources.

In digital contexts, organizations use technological capabilities, agility, and strategic partnerships to develop competitive strategies [ 85 ]. The effectiveness of these strategies depends on employees' motivation, learning orientation, and willingness to adapt. Agile organizations are associated with mobilizing resources, implementing innovative solutions, and adjusting their structures by recognizing threats and opportunities [ 32 ]. Such agility may emerge when employees are supported to experiment, learn, and adapt to challenges. Digital leaders may be associated with competitive advantage through being associated with competencies and supporting learning-oriented environments [ 23 ]. Extending beyond studies that examine direct effects (e.g., [ 48 ]), we propose that digital leadership is associated with resilience primarily through the activation of perceived organizational agility. Thus, agility serves as a mediating mechanism, reflecting how digital leadership relates to adaptive capacity. In this context, the following hypothesis is proposed:

Digitalization is a process in which organizations reshape their strategic priorities to remain competitive. In this process, digital leadership plays a critical role not only in managing technological infrastructure but also in being associated with transforming organizations' innovation capacity, agility, and data-driven decision-making mechanisms [ 33 ]. At the employee level, this transformation depends on how individuals interpret digital change and regulate uncertainty. Digital leaders aim to build agile structures that adapt to dynamic environments while turning technology into a strategic advantage, which is consistent with the Dynamic Capabilities Theory [ 75 ]. Digital leadership is associated with employee sustainable performance through its association with organizations' sensing, seizing, and transforming capabilities. However, these capabilities can be associated with sustained outcomes only when employees are able to respond adaptively, making organizational agility a critical intermediary mechanism.

Jasim et al. [ 35 ] confirmed the positive associations of digital leadership with creativity, agility, and organizational learning. Nevertheless, the direct association between digital leadership and employee sustainable performance may depend on the organization's agility capacity, as agility is associated with enabling technological capabilities to be associated with operational flexibility and innovative applications [ 16 ]. From a perceptual perspective, agility may be associated with employees' ability to adapt and maintain task engagement under changing conditions. Empirical evidence shows that organizations with high agility benefit more from digital investments [ 13 ], suggesting that the performance associations of digital leadership are more likely to be realized in the presence of agility [ 83 ].

From a resource-based view [ 9 ], digital leaders are associated with transforming technology into a valuable resource,however, this resource is related to sustainable advantage only when supported by perceived organizational agility. Agile organizations rapidly implement strategic decisions, adapt to technological change, and respond to customer demands. Mollah et al. [ 54 ] showed that organizations with strong digital leadership but low agility experienced performance decline, whereas highly agile organizations showed enhanced competitive performance. These findings suggest that perceived organizational agility serves as a behavioral and perceptual bridge through which digital leadership is associated with employee sustainable performance. While previous research has established a link between digital leadership and sustainable performance (e.g., [ 44 , 68 ]), the present study argues that this relationship is largely indirect, operating through the agility that digital leaders may foster within their organizations. Accordingly, organizational agility mediates the association between digital leadership and employee sustainable performance.

This study’s theoretical model primarily examines constructs at the organizational level (digital leadership, organizational agility, organizational resilience, and employee sustainable performance). However, the manifestation and effects of these constructs are inevitably shaped through individuals’ mental models, perceptions, and experiences [ 46 ]. From a psychological perspective, higher-level phenomena such as organizational climate, capabilities, and strategic orientation become tangible in the shared perceptions of employees. Therefore, the self-report measures at the individual level in this study were collected based on two key mechanisms that make them valid indicators of organizational-level constructs:

The Referent-Shift Model guides our measurement items rather than asking participants about their personal beliefs or attitudes, the items prompt them to evaluate the characteristics of their organization as a whole (e.g., “The organization I work for adapts quickly to change”). This shifts the referent of the measurement from the individual to the organization, ensuring that the collected data directly reflects the perceived state of organizational-level constructs.

These individual responses ultimately reflect a Shared Unit Property—a perception shaped by the organizational context. Such perceptions are formed through social interactions, leadership communications, and shared experiences within the organization. This provides the theoretical rationale for treating individual-level data as indicative of organizational-level variables [ 11 ]. In this study, organizational agility and resilience are thus conceptualized as manifestations of such collective psychological perceptions.

This research aims to examine the relationships between digital leadership, employee sustainable performance, organizational resilience, and determine the role of organizational agility as a mediating variable in these effects. The estimated model of the research is shown in Fig. 1 .

This study includes public- and private-sector employees, and used convenience sampling to collect the data. To capture contextual variability arising from differences in structural flexibility, leadership practices, and digital maturity, data were collected from employees working in both public and private sector organizations. The sample deliberately includes employees from both public and private sectors, as well as diverse industries (service, healthcare, education, manufacturing, retail). This cross-sectoral sampling strategy was adopted to examine whether the proposed theoretical model holds across different organizational contexts with varying levels of digitalization and structural flexibility, with the aim of enhancing the external validity of the findings. Our aim is not to compare sectors statistically, but to demonstrate that the relationships among digital leadership, agility, resilience, and sustainable performance are not confined to a single sector. The convenience sampling approach was preferred because access to employees actively experiencing digital transformation processes across multiple sectors was prioritized. This approach enabled the inclusion of participants from diverse organizational contexts characterized by different levels of digital maturity, structural flexibility, and leadership practices. Although this sampling strategy limits statistical generalizability, it was considered appropriate for examining perceptual relationships among the study variables across heterogeneous organizational settings.

The selected sectors represent varying levels of digital maturity and structural flexibility: education and healthcare typically operate within more hierarchical and regulation-intensive environments, whereas service and retail sectors tend to exhibit greater operational flexibility and customer-facing digital adoption. Manufacturing occupies an intermediate position, with increasing reliance on Industry 4.0 technologies. This variation was deliberately sought to test whether the proposed relationships hold across different organizational contexts. Nevertheless, the overrepresentation of the education sector and the high proportion of graduate-degree holders suggest that findings may be more reflective of knowledge-intensive, highly educated workforces than of the broader employee population.

The sample consisted of 68.6% women and 31.4% men. In total, 54.5% of participants were married and 45.5% were single. The average age of participants was 36.9 years (SD = 8.48). Participants worked in various sectors: 20.8% in service, 13.5% in health care, 54.2% in education, 3.2% in manufacturing, 2.6% in retail, and 5.8% in other sectors. In terms of education, 1.6% had a high school diploma, 4.2% an associate degree, 27.6% a bachelor’s degree, and 66.7% a graduate degree. All variables were measured through individual employees' perceptions, reflecting perceived organizational agility, resilience, etc. -not objective organization-level metrics. This perceptual approach is consistent with our psychological focus, aiming to capture employees' subjective experiences of their organizational environment. Although constructs are conceptualized at the organizational level, data were collected from individuals based on the premise that organizational phenomena can be assessed through the aggregated perceptions of those who experience them. In doing so, we adopt a fundamentally psychological lens: an organization's "agility" or "resilience" is not an abstract entity but a lived reality in the minds of its members. Measuring these as shared perceptions reflects the psychological essence of these organizational capabilities. To support the validity of this approach, several considerations were integral to the research design. First, all scales employed in this study consist of referent-shift items, which ask participants to rate the characteristics of their organization as a whole, rather than their personal attitudes. Second, the participants in our sample represent a wide range of different organizations across various sectors in Turkiye. Each participant's response therefore serves as a perceptual data point reflecting their unique organizational context. In the analyses, individuals are treated as observers or informants of their organizational environment, and their responses are used as perceptual indicators of organizational characteristics. Consequently, while the level of analysis remains the individual, the independent variables (digital leadership, organizational agility) are modeled as attributes of the individual's organizational context that are hypothesized to be associated with their perceptions of resilience and sustainable performance.

Given the sample structure–-with one or a few participants from each of many different organizations rather than multiple participants from each single organization–-assessing within-group agreement (e.g., via rwg or ICC statistics) was not feasible. This is a common scenario in perceptual climate research, and the issue is addressed by explicitly modeling the organizational context as perceived by individual respondents [ 34 ]. Nevertheless, readers should interpret these findings as reflecting employees' subjective perceptions of their organization's capabilities rather than objective, independently verified organizational attributes. All measurement instruments employed in this study were adopted from previously validated scales reported in the literature and were based on Turkish adaptation studies with established validity and reliability evidence. The use of perceptual self-report measures is consistent with the theoretical perspective of the study, which emphasizes employees’ interpretations and evaluations of organizational leadership and capabilities rather than objective organizational indicators.

Data were collected using an online survey. Participants received survey links via Google Forms. The first page explained the purpose of the study, assured participants of anonymity, and informed them that they could stop responding at any time. Prior to data collection, ethical approval was obtained from Çankaya University (Ethics Committee No. 46, dated 27 June 2024). The survey was distributed via online channels (e.g., WhatsApp, Instagram, Telegram). Data were collected in January–February 2025. Of 354 returned surveys, 42 were discarded due to incomplete or incorrect responses, leaving 312 valid surveys for analysis. Anderson and Gerbing [ 5 ] posit that a minimum sample size of 150 is necessary to ensure robust parameter estimation in structural equation modeling (SEM). Furthermore, ( [ 74 ], p. 482) suggest that variables demonstrating skewness and kurtosis values within the range of ± 1.5 can be considered approximately normally distributed. In the present study, all observed values for skewness and kurtosis fell within these thresholds, thereby satisfying the assumption of normality. Moreover, the sample size ( N = 312) exceeds the recommended minimum for SEM, further supporting the robustness of the analytical approach. In this study, the skewness and kurtosis values fall within the specified range (Table 2 ). In this context, it is concluded that the sample meets the normal distribution condition (at a 95% confidence level) and that the sample size is adequate.
