All Turkish adaptations of the scales used in this study were adopted from previously published validation studies that followed standard cultural adaptation procedures, including translation and back-translation by bilingual experts, expert review, and pilot testing with target samples to ensure linguistic and conceptual equivalence. Scales measuring digital leadership, organizational agility, organizational resilience, and employee sustainable performance were used. Items were rated on a 5-point Likert scale (1 = Strongly disagree to 5 = Strongly agree). A demographic questionnaire collected participants’ gender, marital status, age group, education level and sector of employment at their current institution. Below are details regarding the psychometric properties of the scales:

Developed by Zeike et al. [ 87 ] and adapted into Turkish by Sürücü et al. [ 73 ], the scale consists of six statements and a single dimension. The Cronbach Alpha value of the scale is 0.90. There are no reverse statements in the scale. An example item from the scale is “I can say that my manager is an expert in digital matters.”

Developed by Sharifi and Zhang [ 70 ] and adapted into Turkish by Akkaya and Tabak [ 1 ], the scale consists of four dimensions (8 statements on competence, 3 statements on flexibility, 3 statements on responsiveness, and 3 statements on speed), totaling 17 statements. The Cronbach Alpha value of the scale was found to be 0.92, and the results obtained based on the dimensions were as follows: 0.84 for the competence dimension, 0.81 for the flexibility dimension, 0.74 for the responsiveness dimension, and 0.85 for the speed dimension. There are no reverse statements in the scale. An example item from the scale is the statement, “The organization I work for has a strategic vision that will achieve its long-term goals.”

The Resilience Capacity Scale developed by ( [ 65 ]:139) was used. The scale consists of a total of 21 different statements. The Turkish adaptation and translation of the scale was carried out by the researcher based on Türe and Başar [ 81 ]. The Cronbach Alpha value is 0.92. An example item from the scale is the statement, “It succeeds in acting as a whole with all its employees.”

The scale developed by Ji et al. [ 37 ] and adapted into Turkish by Çilhoroz et al. [ 15 ] was used. The scale consists of 10 statements and a single dimension, with a Cronbach Alpha value of 0.90. There are no reverse statements in the scale. An example item from the scale is the statement “Throughout my entire career, I will always be suitable for my job.”

The data obtained in this study were analyzed using various statistical methods. First, descriptive statistics (means and standard deviations), normality tests, reliability analyses, and Pearson correlations were performed using SPSS 22.0. We measured internal consistency using Cronbach’s alpha. Pearson’s correlation coefficient (range: –1 to 1) was used to examine the direction and strength of linear relationships [ 21 ]. Structural equation modeling (SEM) was conducted using AMOS 24.0 to test the research model. Construct validity was assessed via confirmatory factor analysis (CFA), and fit indices (χ 2 /df, CFI, TLI, etc.) were examined to evaluate model fit [ 10 ]. We then used SEM path analysis to examine the hypothesized relationships. Indirect (mediating) effects were tested via bootstrap analysis (5,000 samples, 95% CI) [ 61 ]. Maximum likelihood estimation was used in SEM.

Confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) was performed to test the construct validity of the scales used in the study. CFA is a statistical technique used to test the suitability of a measurement tool's factor structure to a theoretical framework. This analysis determines how factors are related to observed variables and has a decisive effect on evaluating the structural validity of the measurement tool. CFA reveals the validity of the tool by analyzing factor loadings, goodness-of-fit indices, and inter-factor relationships, and ensures that the validation process is carried out in detail [ 25 ].

Convergent and discriminant validity analyses were conducted to assess construct validity, and scale reliability was evaluated using Cronbach’s alpha. We will present descriptive statistics and correlations for digital leadership, organizational agility, organizational resilience, and employee sustainable performance variables, followed by structural equation modeling results, including the mediating role of organizational agility.

Convergent validity was assessed using average explained variance (AVE) and composite reliability (CR) values. Discriminant validity was analyzed by calculating the square root of the AVE value. According to Fornell and Larcker [ 24 ], the AVE value should be above 0.50 and the CR value should be above 0.70 for composite validity. In terms of discriminant validity, it was emphasized that the square root of the AVE value should be higher than the correlation coefficients with other structures. According to the data presented in Table 3 , the results of the three tests are within the acceptable limits. Additionally, Table 4 shows that the square root of the AVE values are higher than the correlation coefficients between the factors. This indicates that the scales have discriminant validity. While the high inter-construct correlations warrant attention, they align with the theoretical proximity of these dynamic capabilities,the Fornell-Larcker criterion and clear factor structure in CFA support their discriminant validity, suggesting these are strongly related yet distinct constructs as posited by our integrated model. In addition to the Fornell-Larcker criterion, we assessed discriminant validity using the heterotrait-monotrait (HTMT) ratio of correlations [ 31 ]. As shown in Table 5 , all HTMT values were below the more conservative threshold of 0.85 [ 31 ]. Specifically, the HTMT value between organizational agility and resilience was 0.843, while all other inter-construct HTMT values were below 0.76. These results provide further evidence that the constructs, although related, are empirically distinct.

To assess the potential threat of common method variance (CMV), we employed the marker variable approach (Lindell & Whitney, [ 50 ]). A theoretically unrelated random marker variable was included in the model. The correlations between this marker variable and the substantive latent variables were as follows: Digital Leadership ( r = 0.060), Organizational Agility ( r = −0.093), Organizational Resilience ( r = 0.110), and Employee Sustainable Performance ( r = −0.115). All of these correlations were very low and statistically non-significant (p > 0.05). Furthermore, the path coefficients from each substantive construct to the marker variable were all non-significant: Digital Leadership (β = 0.121, t = 1.045, p = 0.296), Organizational Agility (β = −0.290, t = 1.476, p = 0.140), Organizational Resilience (β = 0.236, t = 1.225, p = 0.220), and Employee Sustainable Performance (β = −0.098, t = 1.118, p = 0.264). Taken together with the Harman single-factor test result (which explained 38.8% of the total variance), these findings indicate that common method variance does not pose a serious threat to the validity of our results [ 62 ], (Lindell & Whitney, [ 50 ]).

Within the scope of the study, the internal consistency coefficients of the measurement tools with established construct validity were calculated. Internal consistency was evaluated using Cronbach's Alpha coefficient. In the literature, a Cronbach's Alpha value above 0.70 indicates that the measurement tool has sufficient internal consistency and is therefore reliable [ 21 ]. The Cronbach’s Alpha value of the digital leadership scale included in the study was calculated as 0.95, the organizational agility scale as 0.94, the organizational resilience scale as 0.94, and the employee sustainable performance scale as 0.91. These findings reveal that the Cronbach’s Alpha values of all scales are above the acceptable threshold value specified in the literature and thus support the reliability of the measurement tools in question.

As a result of the first-order CFA, two items were removed due to factor loadings below the threshold of 0.30: item OA16 (organizational agility scale, responsiveness dimension) and item OR4 (organizational resilience scale). No items were deleted from the digital leadership or employee sustainable performance scales. After these deletions, all remaining items demonstrated statistically significant factor loadings ( p < 0.001), and the fit indices for all scales were within acceptable limits (Table 3 ) ([ 45 ]: 219). In the CFA process related to the organizational agility scale, it was determined in the first-order that some fit indices were below the threshold values in the literature. This is because Harrington [ 28 ] states that the factor loading value should be 0.30 or above. In this context, the item with the statement “The organization I work for senses and perceives the direction of change within the scope of environmental change and is prepared for these changes,” which had a factor loading below the specified threshold, was removed from the model. It was determined that the factor loadings of the remaining 16 items were statistically significant ( p < 0.001), and the analyses were re-conducted accordingly. As a result, it was determined that the structural validity of all scales was ensured and that the fit indices were within acceptable limits ( [ 45 ]: 219).

Table 2 presents statistical data showing the mean, standard deviation, normality (skewness and kurtosis) coefficients of the variables and discriminant validity. The mean and standard deviation for digital leadership were 2.66 (SD = 1.01), indicating a slightly below-average perception. Organizational agility had a mean of 2.68 (SD = 0.75), close to average, while organizational resilience had a mean of 2.56 (SD = 0.75), below average. Employee sustainable performance had a mean of 2.03 (SD = 0.51), indicating a low level of perceived sustainable outcomes.

As shown in Table 2 , the mean values of the study variables are relatively low. These descriptive statistics are not the primary focus of our hypothesis tests, but they invite several possible interpretations — none of which are directly tested in this study. One possibility is that sustained exposure to organizational change without adequate support may, in theory, contribute to what some scholars have termed “digital fatigue” or change cynicism, which could dampen employees’ positive evaluations of leadership and capabilities [ 60 ]. Another possibility is that, in challenging economic contexts, employees might prioritize short-term performance over long-term sustainability, which could partly explain the lower sustainable performance scores. A third possibility is that low resilience scores could reflect a perceived lack of psychological safety or collective efficacy in coping with disruptions. We emphasize that these are merely possible explanations, offered as potential directions for future research,they are not empirical findings of the present study. Readers should therefore treat the low mean values as descriptive observations without assigning them a specific causal interpretation based on our data.

To rigorously assess discriminant validity, we employed multiple complementary approaches. First, as shown in Table 4 , the square root of the Average Variance Extracted (AVE) for each construct (digital leadershi p = 0.894; organizational agility = 0.772; organizational resilience = 0.750; employee sustainable performance = 0.777) exceeded the inter-construct correlations, satisfying the Fornell-Larcker criterion [ 24 ]. Second, we calculated the heterotrait-monotrait (HTMT) ratio of correlations [ 31 ]. As presented in Table 5 , all HTMT values were below the conservative threshold of 0.85. Notably, the HTMT value between organizational agility and resilience was 0.843, approaching the threshold—which is theoretically expected given their shared grounding in dynamic capabilities—yet remaining below it, confirming their empirical distinctness. The HTMT value between resilience and sustainable performance was 0.222, well below the threshold, providing strong evidence that employees perceive these as distinct constructs despite their conceptual proximity. These results collectively demonstrate robust discriminant validity across all constructs.

The SEM analysis indicated acceptable model fit (χ 2 /df = 1.638; GFI = 0.91; AGFI = 0.99; NFI = 0.97; TLI = 0.93; CFI = 0.98; RMSEA = 0.045). As presented in Table 6 , digital leadership is positively associated with organizational resilience (β = 0.23, C R = 18.07, p < 0.001) and employee sustainable performance (β = 0.28, C R = 5.59, p < 0.001). Digital leadership was also found to be strongly associated with organizational agility (β = 0.72, C R = 15.28, p < 0.001), which in turn is positively associated with both resilience (β = 0.66, C R = 3.94, p < 0.001) and employee sustainable performance (β = 0.30, C R = 8.36, p < 0.001).

In summary, H1 through H5 were supported. Organizational agility significantly mediated the associations of digital leadership with organizational resilience (H6) and with employee sustainable performance (H7). Digital leadership accounted for 23% of the variance in agility. Together, digital leadership and agility accounted for 74% of the variance in resilience and 72% of the variance in employee sustainable performance. These findings suggest organizational agility's key mediating role in linking digital leadership with organizational resilience and employee sustainable performance. Table 6 presents the values of the standardized (β) path coefficients. Additionally Table 7 shows unstandardized coefficients.

Drawing on employees' perceptual data, this study examined how perceived digital leadership is associated with perceived organizational agility, perceived resilience, and perceived sustainable performance. Our findings indicate that perceived digital leadership is positively and significantly associated with perceived organizational agility, resilience, and employee sustainable performance. Consistent with Dynamic Capabilities Theory, organizational agility significantly mediates the relationship between digital leadership and both resilience and sustainable performance, suggesting that digital leadership is associated with the organization's perceived ability to reconfigure internal processes in response to environmental change. Digital leadership may also be associated with organizations becoming more open to change and effective in leveraging technology. While these findings align with prior studies [ 38 , 59 ], our integrated model extends this literature by positioning agility not merely as an outcome but as a central mediating mechanism through which digital leadership is associated with long-term organizational resilience and sustainable performance within the Dynamic Capabilities Theory framework.

Our findings align with and extend recent work on leadership and adaptive capabilities. Zhang et al. [ 88 ] found that digital leadership was positively associated with improvisational ability and emotional commitment through flow at work, with psychological safety as a moderator. Our study complements this by showing that organizational agility — a shared perceptual outcome — mediates the relationship between digital leadership and both resilience and sustainable performance. While Zhang et al. [ 88 ] focused on individual-level outcomes, we demonstrate that digital leadership is associated with organizational-level perceptions of agility. Similarly, Zhang et al. [ 89 ] reported that responsible leadership was positively associated with sustainable performance through exploitation and exploration knowledge search, with work morale moderating only exploration-related behaviors. Our study extends this by identifying agility as a higher-order mediating capability that subsumes both exploration and exploitation dynamics. Finally, Khan et al. [ 42 , 43 ] found that digital leadership was positively associated with sustainable performance through circular economy practices and technological innovation. Our study adds to this by showing that agility is an additional, distinct mediator that operates even in regular operating environments (not only during crises or innovation-specific contexts). Collectively, these comparisons suggest that digital leadership’s effects on sustainability and resilience are transmitted through multiple psychological and behavioral pathways, with agility serving as a central integrating mechanism. This psychological interpretation is further supported by recent evidence showing that job burnout is associated with lower posttraumatic growth among healthcare workers through diminished psychological resilience and less positive stress beliefs [ 52 ], and that proactive personality enhances individual resilience behaviour through cultural intelligence and global mindset [ 58 ].

While prior research has examined pairwise relationships—such as digital leadership with agility [ 38 ] or agility with resilience [ 3 ]—in isolation, our study's primary contribution lies in integrating these lines of inquiry into a coherent sequential model. We suggest that agility is not merely a parallel outcome of digital leadership but functions as a mechanism linking leadership to both adaptive and performance outcomes. This integration helps clarify how digital leadership is associated with long-term organizational effectiveness.

The second finding is that digital leadership is positively and significantly associated with organizational resilience. This finding indicates that digital leadership is associated with an organization's ability to withstand crises, uncertainties, and sudden environmental changes. Digital leaders' abilities to develop technology-based solutions, make rapid decisions, and foster knowledge-driven management may be associated with an organization's capacity to cope with challenging conditions. These findings suggest that digital leadership is associated not only with innovation and transformation but also with maintaining organizational continuity and stability. This result is consistent with prior research linking digital leadership and resilience [ 48 ].

Third, digital leadership is significantly associated with employee sustainable performance, suggesting a potential positive association with sustainability outcomes. Digital leaders are associated with facilitating technological adoption, innovation, and agile adaptation to environmental changes, which may be associated with employee sustainable performance. However, the strategic orientations provided by digital leadership may be associated with long-term success and sustainability. Accordingly, higher levels of perceived digital leadership may be associated with higher levels of employee sustainable performance.

There are some studies in the literature that address the relationship between digital leadership and employee sustainable performance [ 2 , 7 , 20 , 44 , 68 , 71 ]. These research findings are consistent with the results of previous studies. However, Yahya et al. [ 86 ] found a positive but non-significant effect of digital leadership on employee sustainable performance, which contradicts our results. This discrepancy may arise from their limited sample of public-sector employees and the early stage of digital transformation in that context. Additionally, contextual constraints in public-sector settings may weaken the relationship between leadership and employee-level outcomes, suggesting that the role of agility as a mediator may be particularly important. This highlights the need to investigate contextual factors that moderate the digital leadership-performance link. In this context, digital leadership practices may not yet be sufficiently established or systematically implemented within organizations. In addition, the early stages of digital transformation processes may prevent digital leadership behaviors from directly reflecting on employee sustainable performance. This situation may have prevented the effect of digital leadership on employee sustainable performance from reaching a statistically significant level.

Fourth, organizational agility was significantly associated with resilience, suggesting that agile organizations are more likely to be associated with coping with challenges. The strong correlation is theoretically expected, as both are dynamic capabilities rooted in adaptation [ 77 ]. However, our results support their conceptual distinctness (Fornell-Larcker criterion, HTMT < 0.85), aligning with our theoretical distinction: agility is the proactive capacity to sense and respond swiftly to opportunities, whereas resilience is the reactive and absorptive capacity to withstand and recover from adversities. Thus, agile structures are associated with an organization's preparedness and long-term resilience.

Fifth, organizational agility is significantly and positively associated with employee sustainable performance, suggesting that agility is associated with sustainable success. Agile organizations may be associated with long-term performance through adapting to changes and innovating. This aligns with Teece [ 75 ], who argues that efficient resource use and rapid strategic adaptation are associated with sustained success. In this context, organizational agility may be an important factor associated with employee sustainable performance. Some studies in the literature address the relationship between organizational agility and employee sustainable performance [ 36 , 40 , 41 ]. Therefore, the results of this study are consistent with previous findings.

Sixth, organizational agility mediates the relationship between digital leadership and resilience. In other words, digital leadership is associated with resilience primarily through organizational agility. Digital leaders may be associated with rapid adaptation [ 67 ], and agility may be associated with strengthening this relationship. This finding is consistent with a core tenet of Dynamic Capabilities Theory: in turbulent environments, leadership's strategic value is reflected in building adaptive capacities like agility, rather than being directly associated with outcomes. It also provides additional support for studies examining indirect mechanisms (e.g., [ 48 ]).

Finally, agility also mediates the digital leadership–sustainable performance relationship. This suggests that digital leadership is associated with employee sustainable performance primarily through organizational agility. From a dynamic capabilities perspective [ 77 ], digital leadership is associated with an organization's ability to adapt and innovate. Organizational agility may be associated with the effective use of these capabilities, thereby being associated with employee sustainable performance. In this context, it can be argued that the directions provided by digital leadership may increase the likelihood of organizations achieving sustainable success through organizational agility.

While Lathabhavan and Kuppusamy [ 48 ] highlight the importance of digital leadership during crises (e.g., COVID-19), our results suggest that this relationship operates through a more nuanced mechanism . To clarify, our study differs in three ways: (i) it identifies organizational agility (not empowerment) as the mediator, which is more directly aligned with Dynamic Capabilities Theory,(ii) it examines dual outcomes (resilience and sustainable performance); and (iii) it interprets agility and resilience as perceptual constructs, extending DCT beyond purely structural considerations.

From a theoretical standpoint, this study extends Dynamic Capabilities Theory by highlighting organizational agility as a mediating mechanism between digital leadership and both organizational resilience and employee sustainable performance. Overall, the findings suggest that digital leadership is associated with organizational outcomes through shared perceptions of agility. However, as underlying psychological processes were not directly measured, these interpretations should be considered with caution.

The mediating role of agility suggests that digital leadership is associated with sustainable outcomes when organizations are able to translate leadership-driven initiatives into adaptive practices. This aligns with perspectives emphasizing that sustained performance under dynamic conditions depends on individuals' ability to cope with ongoing change. Accordingly, resilience can be understood not only as structural capacity but also as a collective capability enabling organizations to maintain functioning over time.

By integrating digital leadership, agility, and resilience in a single model, this study highlights how leadership-driven digital transformation is associated with organizational and employee-level outcomes. Despite low mean values, the significant relationships indicate that differences in employees' perceptions are meaningfully associated with differences in organizational outcomes.

When evaluated within the context of Turkiye, the findings suggest that certain cultural and structural factors may have influenced the results. The dominant hierarchical organizational structures, particularly in public institutions and some private sector organizations, may act as constraints on agility. Moreover, although the importance of digital transformation has increased, many leaders may lack sufficient awareness to fully implement this transformation at a strategic level, which may limit the impact of digital leadership. Furthermore, recent economic and environmental uncertainties have increased the importance of organizational resilience. Therefore, these contextual factors may represent relevant background conditions shaping the findings. While these interpretations are consistent with the broader literature on digital transformation in emerging economies, they are offered as plausible rather than definitive explanations. From a theoretical perspective, this study contributes to the digital leadership and organizational psychology literature in several ways. First, it strengthens the integration between Dynamic Capabilities Theory and Upper Echelons Theory by conceptualizing digital leadership as an upper-echelon antecedent associated with organizational adaptation processes. Second, the findings support the conceptualization of organizational agility as the perceptual manifestation of dynamic capabilities rather than a higher-order capability itself. Third, by demonstrating the mediating role of agility, the study provides a more nuanced explanation of how digital leadership is associated with organizational resilience and employee sustainable performance. In doing so, the study extends prior research that has primarily examined these relationships in isolation.

This study has several limitations. First, convenience sampling and voluntary participation limit generalizability. The education sector is overrepresented (54.2%), potentially biasing results as educational institutions often differ in structure, digital maturity, and leadership practices. The sample is demographically homogeneous, with 66.7% holding graduate degrees, which may influence perceptions of digital leadership, agility, and sustainability. Thus, findings may reflect dynamics specific to highly educated professionals in education-related contexts rather than the broader workforce. Sector-specific or controlled analyses were not conducted, further constraining external validity. Caution is advised when generalizing to sectors like manufacturing, retail, or healthcare. Furthermore, our sample includes both public and private sector employees without controlling for sectoral differences. Because we did not conduct multigroup analyses or include sector as a control variable, the generalizability of our findings across sectors remains limited.

Second, the cross-sectional design of the study limits the ability to make causal inferences about the relationships between digital leadership, organizational agility, employee sustainable performance, and organizational resilience. Accordingly, the relationships identified in this study should be interpreted as associative rather than causal. In addition, because all variables were collected from the same respondents at a single point in time, common method variance may represent a potential source of bias. Although the marker variable approach suggested that CMV was unlikely to represent a serious threat, some degree of perceptual inflation cannot be fully excluded in self-report research.

Third, all variables included in the study were obtained using self-report-based measurement tools and the same data collection method. This situation poses a risk of self-report bias in the relationships between variables due to participants' social desirability tendencies, self-awareness levels, or perceptual evaluations. While this approach is common and justifiable in psychological and perceptual research—as it directly captures employees' subjective experiences and interpretations—it also introduces potential perceptual bias and raises questions about ecological validity. Specifically, our measures reflect perceived organizational attributes (e.g., perceived agility, perceived leadership) rather than objective organizational facts. Therefore, the findings should be interpreted as reflecting employees’ perceptions rather than objective organizational realities. Although these perceptions are central to our theoretical model, which posits that psychological evaluations drive outcomes, complementary objective indicators (e.g., archival performance data or third-party assessments) would strengthen the robustness of the findings.

Furthermore, although the measurement tools used in the current research are based on Turkish adaptation and validity-reliability studies, the fact that the relevant concepts were largely developed in different cultural contexts may create some limitations in terms of cross-cultural validity. Accordingly, potential limitations regarding conceptual equivalence across different cultural contexts should be considered.

In addition, a conceptual and methodological consideration regarding the level of analysis is warranted. This study examines organizational-level constructs, such as organizational agility and resilience, using perceptual data from individual employees. The theoretical framework—relying on referent-shift scales and the premise that collected perceptions reflect shared contextual properties—supports this approach. However, it should be remembered that the findings reflect employees' aggregated psychological perceptions of their organizations' capabilities and should not be interpreted as direct, objective measurements of macro-level organizational attributes. Furthermore, due to the sample structure (with one or a few participants per organization), we were unable to compute within-group agreement statistics (e.g., rwg(j)) or employ multilevel modeling to formally partition variance across individual and organizational levels. Consequently, the results represent associations among perceived constructs at the individual level of analysis, and inferences about true organizational-level properties require caution. Therefore, interpretations regarding organizational-level conclusions should be made with caution.

The study relies on self-reported measures, which capture employees’ subjective perceptions rather than objective indicators. At the same time, this approach is consistent with psychological research emphasizing individuals’ cognitive and affective evaluations of leadership, agility, and performance. Additionally, data were collected during a period of ongoing digital transformation, which may have influenced respondents’ cautious evaluations and relatively low mean values. In this regard, the relatively low mean scores observed in some variables should be interpreted with caution, as they may reflect contextual conditions rather than stable organizational characteristics. Perceived low sustainable performance can also stem from a lack of empathetic change management. When leaders mandate digital transformations without adequate support, training, or psychological preparation, employees may perceive change as a threat rather than an opportunity, leading to a defensive retreat instead of agile engagement. Future research could directly examine the psychological mechanisms (e.g., psychological safety, collective efficacy) that might underlie the relationships observed in this study.

When evaluated within the context of Turkiye, the findings suggest that certain cultural and structural factors may have influenced the results. Furthermore, the economic crises, political uncertainties, and global events such as the COVID-19 pandemic that Turkiye has faced over the past decade have increased the importance of organizational resilience. This study was conducted in Türkiye. Future research in different cultural or economic contexts may reveal how contextual factors moderate the observed relationships.

Future research should directly test the psychological micro-foundations proposed in our theoretical model—such as psychological safety, collective efficacy, and shared sensemaking—which were not empirically examined in this study. These mechanisms could deepen understanding of how perceived agility and resilience emerge. Multilevel designs may help capture how such processes operate across individual and team levels to shape these perceptions.

Beyond psychological mechanisms, organizational factors (e.g., culture, motivation, job satisfaction) warrant investigation as potential moderators of digital leadership across hierarchical levels and institutional contexts. Methodologically, qualitative studies could explore the dynamic interplay between digital leadership and agility, while longitudinal designs could trace their co-evolution over time. To mitigate common method bias, researchers should consider multi-source data (e.g., combining employee perceptions with leader evaluations or archival metrics) and temporal separation of measurements. More representative sampling across sectors and demographic groups would improve generalizability, and sector-specific comparisons could clarify boundary conditions.

Additionally, the role of digital transformation architectures, competence development, and adaptive leadership models in fostering sustainability merits further inquiry. The relational dimensions of resilience—including social capital, knowledge flow, and engagement—also offer valuable avenues for future research.

To enhance scholarly value, subsequent studies should adopt longitudinal, cross-cultural, and industry-specific designs. Longitudinal research can examine how the relationships among perceived digital leadership, agility, resilience, and sustainable performance evolve over time, thereby clarifying causal direction and temporal dynamics. Cross-cultural studies would test the robustness of our mediation model across different national and institutional contexts, particularly in countries with varying digital infrastructure, power distance, and uncertainty avoidance. Industry-specific comparisons (e.g., manufacturing versus education versus healthcare) could identify contextual boundary conditions shaped by different levels of digital maturity. Such extensions would not only validate the generalizability of our findings but also inform tailored interventions for diverse organizational settings.

The findings indicate that digital transformation initiatives alone, without complementary organizational adjustments, are unlikely to generate sustainable outcomes. Organizations benefit most when digital leadership practices foster adaptive conditions that support agility and resilience. Accordingly, digital leadership should be viewed not merely as a technological competency but as a strategic organizational capability associated with long-term adaptability and sustainability.

To operationalize digital leadership capabilities in dynamic environments, organizational leaders may consider five actionable strategies. First, they should embed digital agility into leadership competency frameworks. Rather than treating digital leadership as a standalone technical skill, organizations should integrate digital sensing, seizing, and reconfiguring capabilities into existing leadership development programmes. This includes training leaders to recognize weak signals of environmental change, use real-time data analytics for decision-making, and empower teams to experiment with digital tools without fear of failure. Second, leaders should foster structural flexibility through cross-functional digital teams. Establishing temporary, cross-functional task forces empowered to redesign workflows, test new technologies, and scale successful pilots across the organization enables rapid iteration and learning, provided these teams have clear mandates and access to resources. Third, organizations should implement feedback loops that translate employee perceptions into strategic action. Given that perceived agility mediates leadership outcomes, regularly surveying employees' perceptions of digital leadership, agility, and resilience can inform targeted interventions, such as improving internal communication, reducing bureaucratic bottlenecks, or providing psychological safety for experimentation. Fourth, developing crisis-preparedness routines that leverage digital capabilities is essential. Simulating disruption scenarios—for example, supply chain shocks, cyberattacks, or market shifts—allows organizations to stress-test their digital leadership and agility responses, and scenario-based training helps leaders internalize adaptive behaviours before actual crises occur. Fifth, organizations should align performance metrics with agility and resilience outcomes. Traditional performance indicators often prioritize short-term efficiency over long-term adaptability; therefore, leaders should incorporate metrics such as speed of response to market changes, cross-functional collaboration effectiveness, and employee-reported readiness for digital transformation into performance evaluation systems.

Beyond these structural and behavioural strategies, leadership development programmes should prioritize digital competencies, strategic vision, and change management skills. When selecting digital leaders, organizations should emphasize not only technical expertise but also strategic thinking, effective communication, and the ability to motivate employees throughout transformation processes.

The findings also reveal relatively low levels of perceived employee sustainable performance. Practitioners should therefore integrate sustainability goals more explicitly into holistic digital transformation strategies. Financial pressures and economic uncertainty often lead organizations to prioritize short-term needs, undermining long-term sustainability initiatives. Strategic planning processes should explicitly address these resource-related constraints, enabling the development of support mechanisms that facilitate both sustainability adoption and long-term competitiveness.

Finally, to fully leverage agility as a strategic capability, organizations should establish flexible processes and agile decision-making mechanisms. Streamlined decision-making structures enable rapid crisis response, while encouraging quick adaptation to feedback. Investing in systems that support continuous learning, responsiveness, and rapid adjustment is essential for sustaining performance in the digital age.

This study involved human participants. Prior to data collection, ethical approval was obtained from the Ethics Committee of Çankaya University (Approval No: 46, dated 27 June 2024). All participants were informed about the purpose and scope of the research and provided written informed consent before participating in the interviews. The study was conducted in accordance with the ethical principles of the Declaration of Helsinki.

Digital disruption has transformed organizations [ 79 ]. In today's rapidly evolving technological landscape, organizations need leaders who can keep up with digital developments to survive. Leaders' ability to navigate the digital world is associated with organizational success [ 19 ].

Digital leadership, derived from Hambrick and Mason's [ 27 ] Upper Echelons Theory, refers to the integration of leadership skills and digital competencies to leverage digital technologies for organizational change and innovation [ 22 , 84 ]. Such leaders are also associated with encouraging innovative approaches among employees, which in turn is associated with increased motivation and performance [ 19 ].

From an organizational psychology perspective, leadership behaviors go beyond being merely a set of actions; they are actively interpreted and understood psychologically by employees. This interpretation process occurs through collective psychological filters such as perceptions of psychological safety and organizational climate [ 17 , 69 ]. Ultimately, this process is associated with how employees interpret uncertainty, respond to change, and regulate their work-related behaviors. Recent studies have examined psychological mechanisms linking digital leadership to outcomes (e.g., [ 42 , 43 , 88 , 89 ]. The present study, however, focuses on organizational agility as a mediating mechanism within Dynamic Capabilities Theory, without directly measuring these psychological processes.

In organizations undergoing digital transformation, employees continuously evaluate leaders’ digital competencies in terms of perceived support, transparency, and responsiveness. These evaluations are associated with collective meaning-making processes, which in turn are associated with employees’ psychological readiness to adapt and learn [ 60 ]. Accordingly, perceived organizational agility and resilience may reflect shared psychological perceptions that are associated with reduced uncertainty and with sustainable performance [ 30 ].

Digital leadership is defined as a strategic approach that is associated with promoting innovation and collaboration through the effective use of technology, which in turn is associated with increased organizational efficiency and productivity [ 80 ]. This approach is not only associated with strengthening decision-making processes and contributing to organizational goals, but also is associated with employees' psychological experiences arising from their interaction with technology (in the context of basic needs such as autonomy, competence, and connectedness).

Organizational agility is a dynamic capability defined as the ability to quickly adapt to changing environmental conditions and deliver innovative, customer-centric solutions [ 32 ]. From a psychological perspective, this capability is associated with a mindset based on the collective tolerance of organizational members towards uncertainty and their interpretation of change as a learning opportunity rather than a threat. Organizational resilience, on the other hand, is the ability to quickly overcome crises, reallocate resources, optimize processes, and harmonize relationships, transforming challenges into growth opportunities [ 12 ]. These capabilities are also associated with employees’ ability to cope with stress and adapt to changing conditions.

Through digital transformation, organizations can not only respond quickly to crises but also are associated with improved employee sustainable performance while fulfilling their environmental responsibilities [ 71 ]. Recent studies, such as Lathabhavan and Kuppusamy [ 48 ], have demonstrated that digital leadership is associated with organizational resilience. However, these studies primarily focus on direct or single-mediator effects. In contrast, the present study extends this line of inquiry by proposing a dual mediation model in which organizational agility serves as the key mechanism through which digital leadership is simultaneously associated with both organizational resilience and employee sustainable performance. Unlike Lathabhavan and Kuppusamy [ 48 ], who examined employee empowerment as a mediator and organizational performance as the sole outcome in Indian SMEs during the acute COVID-19 crisis, our study introduces organizational agility as the mediating mechanism and models dual outcomes (resilience and sustainable performance) in a regular operating environment. Furthermore, while they drew on Conservation of Resources theory, we ground our model in Dynamic Capabilities Theory while considering psychological interpretations as a complementary perspective.

Nevertheless, the mechanisms through which digital leadership may be associated with employee sustainable performance and resilience have not been sufficiently investigated in a single integrated model. Furthermore, while the individual links between these constructs have been explored, there is a need for comprehensive models that integrate digital leadership, agility, resilience, and sustainable performance to clarify the underlying pathways, particularly the dual mediating role of agility.

This gap necessitates a deeper understanding of the human and psychological dimensions of digital transformation within an integrated framework. Moreover, the transformative impact of digitalization extends beyond internal capabilities, actively reshaping how organizations create value and engage with their broader ecosystem [ 26 ]. Consequently, we propose and test an integrated model (Fig. 1 ) grounded in Dynamic Capabilities Theory and organizational psychology. The model posits that digital leadership is positively associated with resilience and sustainable performance. It is associated with shared perceptions of agility and resilience, with agility serving as the observable manifestation of dynamic capabilities [ 75 ]. Thus, agility functions as the key mechanism through which digitally driven leadership is associated with tangible outcomes.

In order to adapt to constantly changing environmental conditions, organizations need to effectively manage the processes of integrating, directing, and restructuring their resources and competencies. Dynamic Capabilities Theory states that in uncertain and rapidly changing environments, organizations cannot rely solely on existing resources. In this context, organizations need to develop strategic flexibility to gain a sustainable competitive advantage [ 77 ].

Dynamic capabilities focus on the processes by which organizations perceive, evaluate, and transform their structures for sustainable competitive advantage through environmental opportunities [ 42 , 43 ]. Perceived digital leadership, through its strategic vision and technology-driven decision-making processes, is associated with building upon these foundations, and may be associated with fostering perceptual alertness and a learning mindset [ 83 ]. Dynamic capabilities are associated with organizational agility by accelerating strategic decision-making in uncertain market conditions [ 76 ],they are also associated with organizational resilience by providing flexible response capacity in crises [ 49 ].

From a psychological standpoint, these dynamic capabilities can be interpreted as being reflected in employees' shared cognitive schemas, collective interpretations of change, and motivation to engage in adaptive behaviors. The present study does not directly measure these cognitive and affective mechanisms; rather, it focuses on their hypothesized perceptual outcomes—namely, perceived organizational agility and resilience. Accordingly, these mechanisms are considered as a theoretical perspective and as potential avenues for future research. Recent empirical studies have explicitly modelled agility as a mediating dynamic capability pathway to resilience, whether in the context of resource scarcity [ 57 ], adaptive marketing capabilities during crises [ 4 ], or employee-level digital work engagement [ 8 ]. The micro-foundations of dynamic capabilities increasingly emphasize employee cognition and affect. Zhang et al. [ 89 ] show that digital leadership induces flow at work, enhancing cognitive flexibility (improvisational ability) and affective attachment (emotional commitment)—states critical for DCT's sensing and seizing processes. Zhang, Akhtar, et al. [ 88 ] demonstrate that responsible leadership drives exploitation and exploration knowledge search behaviors, directly supporting transforming capacity. Khan et al. [ 42 , 43 ]further link digital leadership to circular economy practices as tangible outcomes of dynamic capability deployment. Collectively, these studies suggest that digital leadership activates dynamic capabilities through interpretive pathways—shared perceptions of psychological safety, collective efficacy, and meaning-making— which suggest potential interpretive pathways that may underlie the relationships examined in our mediation model. Future research is needed to test these proposed mechanisms directly. Therefore, while Dynamic Capabilities Theory provides the overarching framework for why organizations need to adapt, this study adopts the view that the how of adaptation may involve employees' collective interpretations of leaders' actions and environmental shifts.

These capabilities link employee sustainable performance to organizational learning and long-term value creation [ 29 ]. In digitally intensive environments, leaders play a critical role not only in initiating technological change but also in enabling organizations to recognize emerging opportunities, respond rapidly to environmental uncertainty, and reconfigure internal processes accordingly. From this perspective, digital leadership functions as a strategic managerial capability that facilitates organizational adaptation and renewal. Organizational agility represents the perceptual and behavioral manifestation of these dynamic processes, reflecting the organization’s ability to respond flexibly and effectively to changing demands. In turn, resilience emerges as a longer-term strategic outcome of these adaptive capabilities, enabling organizations to maintain continuity and recover from disruptions under conditions of uncertainty.

Thus, digital leadership is conceptualized as an antecedent influencing employees’ perceptions of their organizational environment, which subsequently manifest as perceived organizational agility. Organizational resilience, conversely, centers on the reactive and absorptive capacity to withstand, recover from, and adapt following adversities or crises, emphasizing robustness, bounce-back ability, and sustained functioning. While agility is about navigating change for competitive advantage, resilience is about enduring disruption for survival and continuity. This theoretical distinction justifies their treatment as separate constructs in our model, a position supported by our empirical assessment of discriminant validity.

Digitalization is a process in which organizations reshape their strategic priorities to remain competitive. In this process, digital leadership plays a critical role not only in managing technological infrastructure but also in being associated with transforming organizations' innovation capacity, agility, and data-driven decision-making mechanisms [ 33 ]. At the employee level, this transformation depends on how individuals interpret digital change and regulate uncertainty. Digital leaders aim to build agile structures that adapt to dynamic environments while turning technology into a strategic advantage, which is consistent with the Dynamic Capabilities Theory [ 75 ]. Digital leadership is associated with employee sustainable performance through its association with organizations' sensing, seizing, and transforming capabilities. Jasim et al. [ 35 ] confirmed the positive associations of digital leadership with creativity, agility, and organizational learning. From a perceptual perspective, agility may be associated with employees' ability to adapt and maintain task engagement under changing conditions. Empirical evidence shows that organizations with high agility benefit more from digital investments [ 13 ], suggesting that the performance associations of digital leadership are more likely to be realized in the presence of agility [ 83 ].

From a resource-based view [ 9 ], digital leaders are associated with transforming technology into a valuable resource,however, this resource is related to sustainable advantage only when supported by perceived organizational agility. [ 54 ] showed that organizations with strong digital leadership but low agility experienced performance decline, whereas highly agile organizations showed enhanced competitive performance. These findings suggest that perceived organizational agility serves as a behavioral and perceptual bridge through which digital leadership is associated with employee sustainable performance. While previous research has established a link between digital leadership and sustainable performance (e.g., [ 44 , 68 ]), the present study argues that this relationship is largely indirect, operating through the agility that digital leaders may foster within their organizations. Accordingly, organizational agility mediates the association between digital leadership and employee sustainable performance.

From a psychological perspective, higher-level phenomena such as organizational climate, capabilities, and strategic orientation become tangible in the shared perceptions of employees. The Referent-Shift Model guides our measurement items rather than asking participants about their personal beliefs or attitudes, the items prompt them to evaluate the characteristics of their organization as a whole (e.g., “The organization I work for adapts quickly to change”). This shifts the referent of the measurement from the individual to the organization, ensuring that the collected data directly reflects the perceived state of organizational-level constructs.

These individual responses ultimately reflect a Shared Unit Property—a perception shaped by the organizational context. Such perceptions are formed through social interactions, leadership communications, and shared experiences within the organization. This study includes public- and private-sector employees, and used convenience sampling to collect the data. To capture contextual variability arising from differences in structural flexibility, leadership practices, and digital maturity, data were collected from employees working in both public and private sector organizations. The sample deliberately includes employees from both public and private sectors, as well as diverse industries (service, healthcare, education, manufacturing, retail). This cross-sectoral sampling strategy was adopted to examine whether the proposed theoretical model holds across different organizational contexts with varying levels of digitalization and structural flexibility, with the aim of enhancing the external validity of the findings. Our aim is not to compare sectors statistically, but to demonstrate that the relationships among digital leadership, agility, resilience, and sustainable performance are not confined to a single sector. The convenience sampling approach was preferred because access to employees actively experiencing digital transformation processes across multiple sectors was prioritized. This approach enabled the inclusion of participants from diverse organizational contexts characterized by different levels of digital maturity, structural flexibility, and leadership practices. Although this sampling strategy limits statistical generalizability, it was considered appropriate for examining perceptual relationships among the study variables across heterogeneous organizational settings.

The selected sectors represent varying levels of digital maturity and structural flexibility: education and healthcare typically operate within more hierarchical and regulation-intensive environments, whereas service and retail sectors tend to exhibit greater operational flexibility and customer-facing digital adoption. Manufacturing occupies an intermediate position, with increasing reliance on Industry 4.0 technologies. This variation was deliberately sought to test whether the proposed relationships hold across different organizational contexts. Nevertheless, the overrepresentation of the education sector and the high proportion of graduate-degree holders suggest that findings may be more reflective of knowledge-intensive, highly educated workforces than of the broader employee population.

All variables were measured through individual employees' perceptions, reflecting perceived organizational agility, resilience, etc. -not objective organization-level metrics. This perceptual approach is consistent with our psychological focus, aiming to capture employees' subjective experiences of their organizational environment. Although constructs are conceptualized at the organizational level, data were collected from individuals based on the premise that organizational phenomena can be assessed through the aggregated perceptions of those who experience them. In doing so, we adopt a fundamentally psychological lens: an organization's "agility" or "resilience" is not an abstract entity but a lived reality in the minds of its members. Measuring these as shared perceptions reflects the psychological essence of these organizational capabilities. To support the validity of this approach, several considerations were integral to the research design. First, all scales employed in this study consist of referent-shift items, which ask participants to rate the characteristics of their organization as a whole, rather than their personal attitudes. Second, the participants in our sample represent a wide range of different organizations across various sectors in Turkiye. Each participant's response therefore serves as a perceptual data point reflecting their unique organizational context. In the analyses, individuals are treated as observers or informants of their organizational environment, and their responses are used as perceptual indicators of organizational characteristics. Consequently, while the level of analysis remains the individual, the independent variables (digital leadership, organizational agility) are modeled as attributes of the individual's organizational context that are hypothesized to be associated with their perceptions of resilience and sustainable performance.

Given the sample structure–-with one or a few participants from each of many different organizations rather than multiple participants from each single organization–-assessing within-group agreement (e.g., via rwg or ICC statistics) was not feasible. This is a common scenario in perceptual climate research, and the issue is addressed by explicitly modeling the organizational context as perceived by individual respondents [ 34 ]. Nevertheless, readers should interpret these findings as reflecting employees' subjective perceptions of their organization's capabilities rather than objective, independently verified organizational attributes. All measurement instruments employed in this study were adopted from previously validated scales reported in the literature and were based on Turkish adaptation studies with established validity and reliability evidence. The use of perceptual self-report measures is consistent with the theoretical perspective of the study, which emphasizes employees’ interpretations and evaluations of organizational leadership and capabilities rather than objective organizational indicators.

The data obtained in this study were analyzed using various statistical methods. First, descriptive statistics (means and standard deviations), normality tests, reliability analyses, and Pearson correlations were performed using SPSS 22.0. We measured internal consistency using Cronbach’s alpha. Pearson’s correlation coefficient (range: –1 to 1) was used to examine the direction and strength of linear relationships [ 21 ]. Structural equation modeling (SEM) was conducted using AMOS 24.0 to test the research model. Construct validity was assessed via confirmatory factor analysis (CFA), and fit indices (χ 2 /df, CFI, TLI, etc.) were examined to evaluate model fit [ 10 ]. We then used SEM path analysis to examine the hypothesized relationships. Indirect (mediating) effects were tested via bootstrap analysis (5,000 samples, 95% CI) [ 61 ]. Maximum likelihood estimation was used in SEM.

Confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) was performed to test the construct validity of the scales used in the study. CFA is a statistical technique used to test the suitability of a measurement tool's factor structure to a theoretical framework. This analysis determines how factors are related to observed variables and has a decisive effect on evaluating the structural validity of the measurement tool. CFA reveals the validity of the tool by analyzing factor loadings, goodness-of-fit indices, and inter-factor relationships, and ensures that the validation process is carried out in detail [ 25 ].

Convergent and discriminant validity analyses were conducted to assess construct validity, and scale reliability was evaluated using Cronbach’s alpha. We will present descriptive statistics and correlations for digital leadership, organizational agility, organizational resilience, and employee sustainable performance variables, followed by structural equation modeling results, including the mediating role of organizational agility.

Convergent validity was assessed using average explained variance (AVE) and composite reliability (CR) values. Discriminant validity was analyzed by calculating the square root of the AVE value. According to Fornell and Larcker [ 24 ], the AVE value should be above 0.50 and the CR value should be above 0.70 for composite validity. In terms of discriminant validity, it was emphasized that the square root of the AVE value should be higher than the correlation coefficients with other structures. According to the data presented in Table 3 , the results of the three tests are within the acceptable limits. Additionally, Table 4 shows that the square root of the AVE values are higher than the correlation coefficients between the factors. This indicates that the scales have discriminant validity. While the high inter-construct correlations warrant attention, they align with the theoretical proximity of these dynamic capabilities,the Fornell-Larcker criterion and clear factor structure in CFA support their discriminant validity, suggesting these are strongly related yet distinct constructs as posited by our integrated model. In addition to the Fornell-Larcker criterion, we assessed discriminant validity using the heterotrait-monotrait (HTMT) ratio of correlations [ 31 ]. As shown in Table 5 , all HTMT values were below the more conservative threshold of 0.85 [ 31 ]. Specifically, the HTMT value between organizational agility and resilience was 0.843, while all other inter-construct HTMT values were below 0.76. These results provide further evidence that the constructs, although related, are empirically distinct.

To assess the potential threat of common method variance (CMV), we employed the marker variable approach (Lindell & Whitney, [ 50 ]). A theoretically unrelated random marker variable was included in the model. The correlations between this marker variable and the substantive latent variables were as follows: Digital Leadership ( r = 0.060), Organizational Agility ( r = −0.093), Organizational Resilience ( r = 0.110), and Employee Sustainable Performance ( r = −0.115). All of these correlations were very low and statistically non-significant (p > 0.05). Furthermore, the path coefficients from each substantive construct to the marker variable were all non-significant: Digital Leadership (β = 0.121, t = 1.045, p = 0.296), Organizational Agility (β = −0.290, t = 1.476, p = 0.140), Organizational Resilience (β = 0.236, t = 1.225, p = 0.220), and Employee Sustainable Performance (β = −0.098, t = 1.118, p = 0.264). Taken together with the Harman single-factor test result (which explained 38.8% of the total variance), these findings indicate that common method variance does not pose a serious threat to the validity of our results [ 62 ], (Lindell & Whitney, [ 50 ]).

Within the scope of the study, the internal consistency coefficients of the measurement tools with established construct validity were calculated. Internal consistency was evaluated using Cronbach's Alpha coefficient. In the literature, a Cronbach's Alpha value above 0.70 indicates that the measurement tool has sufficient internal consistency and is therefore reliable [ 21 ]. The Cronbach’s Alpha value of the digital leadership scale included in the study was calculated as 0.95, the organizational agility scale as 0.94, the organizational resilience scale as 0.94, and the employee sustainable performance scale as 0.91. These findings reveal that the Cronbach’s Alpha values of all scales are above the acceptable threshold value specified in the literature and thus support the reliability of the measurement tools in question.

As a result of the first-order CFA, two items were removed due to factor loadings below the threshold of 0.30: item OA16 (organizational agility scale, responsiveness dimension) and item OR4 (organizational resilience scale). No items were deleted from the digital leadership or employee sustainable performance scales. After these deletions, all remaining items demonstrated statistically significant factor loadings ( p < 0.001), and the fit indices for all scales were within acceptable limits (Table 3 ) ([ 45 ]: 219). This is because Harrington [ 28 ] states that the factor loading value should be 0.30 or above. In this context, the item with the statement “The organization I work for senses and perceives the direction of change within the scope of environmental change and is prepared for these changes,” which had a factor loading below the specified threshold, was removed from the model. It was determined that the factor loadings of the remaining 16 items were statistically significant ( p < 0.001), and the analyses were re-conducted accordingly. As a result, it was determined that the structural validity of all scales was ensured and that the fit indices were within acceptable limits ( [ 45 ]: 219).

Second, we calculated the heterotrait-monotrait (HTMT) ratio of correlations [ 31 ]. As presented in Table 5 , all HTMT values were below the conservative threshold of 0.85. Notably, the HTMT value between organizational agility and resilience was 0.843, approaching the threshold—which is theoretically expected given their shared grounding in dynamic capabilities—yet remaining below it, confirming their empirical distinctness. The HTMT value between resilience and sustainable performance was 0.222, well below the threshold, providing strong evidence that employees perceive these as distinct constructs despite their conceptual proximity. These results collectively demonstrate robust discriminant validity across all constructs.

The SEM analysis indicated acceptable model fit (χ 2 /df = 1.638; GFI = 0.91; AGFI = 0.99; NFI = 0.97; TLI = 0.93; CFI = 0.98; RMSEA = 0.045). As presented in Table 6 , digital leadership is positively associated with organizational resilience (β = 0.23, C R = 18.07, p < 0.001) and employee sustainable performance (β = 0.28, C R = 5.59, p < 0.001). Digital leadership was also found to be strongly associated with organizational agility (β = 0.72, C R = 15.28, p < 0.001), which in turn is positively associated with both resilience (β = 0.66, C R = 3.94, p < 0.001) and employee sustainable performance (β = 0.30, C R = 8.36, p < 0.001).

In summary, H1 through H5 were supported. Organizational agility significantly mediated the associations of digital leadership with organizational resilience (H6) and with employee sustainable performance (H7). Digital leadership accounted for 23% of the variance in agility. Together, digital leadership and agility accounted for 74% of the variance in resilience and 72% of the variance in employee sustainable performance. These findings suggest organizational agility's key mediating role in linking digital leadership with organizational resilience and employee sustainable performance.
